name: Region-beta paradox
statement: People sometimes recover faster from intense distress than from mild distress, because only intense distress crosses the threshold that triggers the defences against it.
meaning: The name comes from a diagram about travel rather than about feeling. Gilbert and colleagues imagine a commuter who walks at 3 miles per hour to destinations under a mile away and cycles at 15 miles per hour to anything further. Plot time against distance and the line breaks at the threshold. Points just past a mile, the stretch labelled region beta, are reached sooner than the furthest point the commuter would have walked to. Time and distance rise together inside each region and reverse across them. The paper carries that shape over to distress. If the processes that dull a bad feeling switch on only once the feeling passes some level, a worse event can leave a person feeling better sooner. Two claims sit inside this. The first is the reversal, that intense states can abate faster than mild ones. The second is the account of why, that defences fire above a threshold and not below it. The paper tests the first and infers the second.

origin.who: Daniel T. Gilbert, Matthew D. Lieberman, Carey K. Morewedge and Timothy D. Wilson
origin.note: The paper names the paradox and reports four experiments under three study numbers. Study 1 asks students to rate imagined transgressions; Studies 2a, 2b and 3 stage an insult in the laboratory. It was received in March 2001 and its revision accepted in January 2003.

evidence: Study 1 asked 98 students, 57 men and 41 women, to imagine nine transgressions, from a polite rejection to a hit-and-run dent in their car. They rated how they would feel about the culprit at the moment and one week later. Intensity and duration estimates correlated at r = .88, p < .01, with no curvilinear component. The paper words that as a correlation across participants and prints nine scenario means in Table 1. Correlations computed within each participant had a mean of .65, SD .30, and a median of .75, with one of the 98 dropped for giving the same duration rating nine times. Study 2a insulted 26 students by having a supposed other participant rate their personality as the worst of three profiles. Students who expected to meet that rater moved further from baseline across eight 125 mm lines than students who did not, a mean change of 28.8 against 13.5, t(24) = 2.075, p < .05. The eight scales had alphas of .82 at baseline and .81 after the insult. Study 2b ran the same insult on 29 students split between forecasting and experiencing. Forecasters expected to like an insulting partner less than an insulting non-partner, 2.83 against 4.57 on a seven-point scale. Five minutes after the insult, experiencers reported the reverse, 4.57 against 3.33. The weighted contrast across the four cells gave t(27) = 3.17, p < .005, and Table 2 marks both cell differences at p < .05. Study 3 added bystanders who saw the same insult delivered to somebody else, 58 students in four cells of 11 to 20. Forecasters expected victims to like the rater less than bystanders would, 3.15 against 3.83. Experiencing victims liked the rater more than bystanders did, 4.33 against 3.36. The weighted contrast gave t(56) = 3.24, p < .01, while Table 3 marks the forecasters' gap at p < .10 and the experiencers' at p < .05.

replication.headline: No repetition of the paper's four experiments was located, though three later literatures test the intensity and duration relation under other names and point different ways.
replication.detail: Searches on 17 August 2026 covered Crossref, Europe PMC full-text search, PubMed, the OSF preprint registry and general web search, and read the titles of the 168 records Semantic Scholar lists as citing the paper. Europe PMC returns one document for the phrase 'region-beta paradox', the original. OpenAlex was rate-limited before its citing list could be read; an earlier pass recorded 145 citing works there. PsycINFO was not searched and is the next place to look. Three lines of work bear on the claim without repeating the studies. Bosson, Pinel and Vandello surveyed 188 students at a university in the central United States about hostile and benevolent sexism. Their abstract reports that people overestimated the impact of hostile sexism and underestimated the impact of benevolent sexism, and mispredicted both the intensity of women's initial reactions and the duration of their recovery, with the intensity error fully accounting for the duration error. Salomon, Burgess and Bosson exposed women to a hostile, a benevolent or a non-sexist remark from a male experimenter. The thesis version of that work reports 124 women recruited and 122 analysed after two equipment failures. Hostile sexism raised cardiovascular reactivity during the task that followed, and benevolent sexism impaired the return to baseline afterwards. That is the shape the paradox predicts, and the thesis offers Gilbert's account as one of three candidate explanations for it, after the fact rather than by design. Verduyn, Delvaux, Van Coillie, Tuerlinckx and Van Mechelen ran two experience-sampling studies on fear, anger, joy, gratitude and sadness episodes. For all five emotions, the higher the intensity at onset, the longer the episode lasted. That is the monotonic relation the paradox says can reverse, measured in daily life and without a threshold contrast.

limits: No study in the paper measured how long a reaction lasted. Studies 2b and 3 took one reading five minutes after the insult and Study 1 collected predictions only, so what was shown is a reversal at a single time point rather than a recovery curve. Nothing measured the defences credited with producing it. Study 2a establishes that the partner insult hurt more, and the attenuating process is read back from the later reversal rather than observed. Cells are small, seven to eight people in Study 2b and 11 to 20 in Study 3. The only effect size the paper reports is Study 1's r = .88, since the reversals in Studies 2b and 3 arrive as means, standard deviations and t values, leaving a replication no standardised figure to aim at. The pain and injury version, that a trick knee outlasts a shattered patella, sits in the introduction as an illustration and carries no data. So do the chocolate, seat-belt and martini examples in the discussion. Eastwick, Finkel, Krishnamurti and Loewenstein followed Northwestern freshmen through the end of a real relationship. Sixty-nine enrolled, and the report rests on the 26 whose relationship ended in the first six months. Distress forecast two weeks before the split was compared against distress reported at the split and 2, 6 and 10 weeks later. Forecast distress exceeded actual distress at the breakup, coefficient .79, t(24) = 4.30, p < .001, and the two trajectories then fell at rates that did not differ, coefficient -.02, t(24) = -0.55, p = .591. People got the starting height wrong and the decay right. That paper cites the 2004 article for the psychological immune system and never names the paradox. Steephen and colleagues built a model of affective adaptation that predicts when the intensity and duration correlation is positive, negative or absent; its abstract says the predictions match existing data, and the paper supplies none of its own. The 2004 discussion dates Trope and Fishbach's counteractive self-control study to 2002, while the volume and pages it gives, 79 and 493 to 506, belong to a paper Crossref records as published in 2000. The copy read here is the author-posted page proof, stamped uncorrected; the published version could not be obtained.
misreadings: The travel illustration is walking against cycling, 3 miles per hour against 15, with the switch at one mile, and region beta names the far stretch reached quickly rather than the mild zone where people get stuck. Retellings blur both halves. Wallet Hacks has the commuter walk one mile and bike two, and drops the speeds. It then defines beta regions as 'those times when we endure a mild irritant longer than we would've tolerated a more serious one', putting the label on the wrong side of the threshold. The paper's other transport line is a flight from New York to London arriving sooner than a drive from New York to Boston. The phrase 'psychological immune system' appears nowhere in it, and the word immune appears once, in the reference to Gilbert, Pinel, Wilson, Blumberg and Wheatley. Eastwick and colleagues cite the 2004 paper for exactly that phrase anyway. It belongs to the immune-neglect work, covered here at entry 161, and importing it makes a metaphor from another article sound like this one's finding. The claim that people bounce back faster from worse things in life is stronger than anything demonstrated here. What was demonstrated is that students liked a rude prospective partner more than a rude non-partner five minutes on.
